hero.text: Four questions, forty marks, forty-five minutes. Each one asks for a different kind of thinking, and the commonest way to lose marks is to answer Question 3 the way you answered Question 2.

blocks.title: Original RCF practice material
text: Every extract, practice question and model answer on this page was written by RCF English. They are **not** AQA questions or AQA source texts, and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced.

AQA's own specimen papers and mark schemes are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/) and are the authoritative guide to the standard. RCF English is not affiliated with or endorsed by AQA.

blocks.text: **Section A of Paper 1 is 40 marks in four questions: 4, 8, 8 and 20.** Question 1 tests whether you can find information. Questions 2 and 3 test whether you can analyse language and structure. Question 4 tests whether you can evaluate - agree or disagree with a statement, and justify it.

blocks.heading: The extract used in the examples below
text: So that the worked examples are about something, here is a short original passage written for this page. It is in the style of the fiction openings Paper 1 uses. **It is not an AQA source.**

parts.heading: From The Long Field (original RCF passage)
text: **Lines 1-7.** The frost had come in the night and taken the field entirely. Where there had been mud and the ruts of the tractor there was now a hard grey sheet, pale as bone, that rang faintly underfoot. The hedges stood black against it. Nothing moved in them. At the far end, where the ground fell away towards the river, a thin mist lay along the hollow and did not lift, though the sun had been up an hour.

**Lines 8-14.** Martha walked out into the middle of it and stopped. She had crossed this field every morning for eleven years and she did not recognise it. The distances were wrong. The gate she was walking towards seemed to have moved further off, and the barn behind her, when she turned, seemed nearer than it had any right to be. She stood there a long moment, turning slowly, and understood at last that it was the silence doing it - that without the ordinary noise of the place she had no way of measuring how far anything was.

**Lines 15-20.** Then the mist at the bottom of the field moved. Not lifted; moved, the whole body of it, sliding a few yards along the hollow the way a sleeper shifts. Martha watched it. She was not frightened, and it interested her that she was not. She thought: I should go back. She thought it quite calmly, the way a person thinks about a task for later in the week, and she did not go back. She began instead to walk down the slope towards the river, and the frost rang under her, and behind her the barn went on standing where it had always stood.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO1: can you find stated information in a defined part of the text? It is the only question on the paper where a correct answer is simply correct. There is no analysis and no credit for style.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 4 marks - one for each thing. **RCF recommendation: about 5 minutes.** AQA gives 45 minutes for the whole section and does not publish a per-question time.

parts.heading: The method
numbered: Underline the line numbers in the question. Everything outside them is worthless here.
Find four separate facts about the stated topic.
Write each as a short phrase. Do not write sentences.
Stop at four. A fifth answer cannot gain a mark and a wrong one may replace a right one.

parts.heading: Worked example
text: *List four things about the field from lines 1 to 7.*
numbered: The frost had covered it in the night.
It had previously been muddy with tractor ruts.
It was hard and grey.
It made a faint ringing sound underfoot.

parts.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Copying a whole sentence that contains the answer instead of stating the fact.
Giving four things about the wrong subject - the hedges, say, rather than the field.
Straying outside the stated lines.
Interpreting. *The field feels lonely* is not a stated thing about the field.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO2: can you explain how the writer's word choices, techniques and sentence forms create an effect? The question names the effect it wants you to write about, and it gives you three bullet prompts - words and phrases, language features and techniques, and sentence forms.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 8 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 10 minutes.** In AQA's specimen mark scheme the top band for this question is 7-8 marks and rewards detailed, perceptive analysis with judicious quotation and accurate terminology.

parts.heading: The method: quotation, technique, effect, development
numbered: Choose three short quotations from the given lines - short enough to embed in your own sentence.
Name what the writer is doing. Use the term only if you are sure of it; a wrong term costs more than no term.
Say what effect it creates *for the reader*.
Develop one of the three further: zoom in on a single word and offer a second reading of it.

parts.heading: Worked example
text: *How does the writer use language in lines 8 to 14 to describe Martha's confusion?*

The writer uses the flat statement "The distances were wrong" to place us inside Martha's confusion rather than outside it. The sentence is only four words long, and after the long descriptive sentence before it the abruptness makes the wrongness feel like something noticed suddenly rather than reasoned out.

The verbs then work against each other. The gate "seemed to have moved further off" while the barn "seemed nearer than it had any right to be". The repetition of "seemed" concedes that neither has actually moved, so the disorientation is located in Martha's perception, not in the field. The phrase "any right to be" is faintly comic and faintly indignant, as though the barn were misbehaving - which suggests Martha is still calm enough to be irritated rather than afraid.

Finally, the writer withholds the explanation until the end of the paragraph: it is "the silence doing it". Because the cause arrives last, the reader experiences the confusion first and understands it afterwards, exactly as Martha does.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: *How does the writer use language in lines 1 to 7 to describe the frost?* Write three developed paragraphs, about 10 minutes.

parts.heading: Indicative answer for the practice task
bullets: **"taken the field entirely"** - the verb makes the frost an occupying force, and "entirely" leaves no part of the field unclaimed.
**"pale as bone"** - a simile that brings death into a description of weather, and "bone" is hard as well as pale, so it does two jobs at once.
**"rang faintly underfoot"** - a sound word used for a surface, which makes the frost feel thin and brittle; "faintly" keeps the whole scene quiet.

**"The hedges stood black against it. Nothing moved in them."** - two short sentences after a long one, the second even shorter, so the stillness is enacted by the sentence lengths as well as described.
**"did not lift, though the sun had been up an hour"** - the concession tells us the ordinary rules are suspended, which prepares for Martha's disorientation later.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO2 again, but structure rather than language. The question asks how the writer has ordered the whole text to interest a reader. It is about the shape of the extract, not its words - which is why answering it with quotations and adjectives is the single commonest way to lose these 8 marks.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 8 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 10 minutes.** The specimen mark scheme's top band, 7-8 marks, rewards detailed and perceptive understanding of structural features and analysis of their effects.

parts.heading: The method: beginning, shift, end
numbered: **Beginning.** What does the writer put in front of you first, and why that?
**Shift.** Where does the focus change - from wide to narrow, outside to inside, place to person, present to past? Name the moment.
**End.** Where are you left, and what has changed since the opening?
Add one further structural feature: a repeated image, a withheld piece of information, a change of sentence rhythm, a shift in time.

parts.heading: Worked example
text: *How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?*

The writer opens on the field rather than on a person. For seven lines there is no one in the extract at all, only frost, hedges and mist, so the reader is given a place and left to wonder who will enter it. That withholding is the first thing that creates interest.

The focus then narrows sharply. Martha walks "out into the middle of it and stopped", and from that point the extract is inside her perception rather than above the field. What we are shown stops being what is there and becomes what she thinks is there - the gate that seems further, the barn that seems nearer. The reader is moved from watching to sharing.

The final paragraph reverses the direction of the whole piece. Everything until then has been about stillness; then "the mist at the bottom of the field moved", and the one thing that moves is the one thing that should not. The writer also structures Martha's decision against expectation: she thinks "I should go back" and then does the opposite in the same sentence, so the extract ends by opening rather than closing.

Underneath all of this the barn is mentioned at the start, in the middle and in the last line, standing "where it had always stood" - a fixed point that measures how far Martha has moved away from the ordinary.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: Take any novel opening you have to hand - two or three pages. Write four sentences: what the writer focuses on first, where the focus shifts, where you are left, and one structural feature that runs through the whole passage. About 10 minutes.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO4: can you evaluate a text critically and support your judgement with references? A student in the extract is quoted making a claim about the second part of the source, and you are asked to what extent you agree. It is worth a quarter of the whole paper.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 20 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 20 minutes** - roughly half the reading section. The specimen mark scheme's top band is 16-20 marks and rewards perceptive, detailed evaluation.

parts.heading: The method
numbered: **Take a position in the first sentence.** Fully agree, largely agree, agree with a qualification - any of these works, but say which.
**Four developed paragraphs**, each one: a point about the statement, a short quotation, an explanation of how the writer created that impression, and your judgement of how well it works.
**Keep the statement in view.** Refer back to its actual wording at least twice.
**Qualify once.** A paragraph beginning *This is less true of...* usually lifts an answer, because evaluation means weighing rather than praising.

parts.heading: Worked example (opening two paragraphs)
text: *A student said: "In the last part of the extract Martha behaves strangely, and the writer makes this feel unsettling rather than dangerous." To what extent do you agree?*

I largely agree, though I would say the writer works harder to make Martha's calm strange than to make the field strange. The unsettling quality comes from the gap between what is happening and how little she minds it.

The clearest evidence is that the writer tells us directly what Martha is not: "She was not frightened, and it interested her that she was not." A more conventional passage would have her afraid, and the refusal is deliberate. By making her curious about her own lack of fear, the writer puts a second layer between Martha and ordinary reaction, and it is that distance, rather than the moving mist, that makes the reader uneasy. The mist itself is described almost gently - it moves "the way a sleeper shifts" - so the threat, if there is one, is not in the landscape.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: *A student said: "The writer makes the field feel like a place where the ordinary rules have stopped working." To what extent do you agree?* Write four developed paragraphs on lines 1 to 14. About 20 minutes.

parts.heading: Indicative content for the practice task
bullets: Agreement: "the distances were wrong"; the gate and barn appearing to move; the mist that "did not lift, though the sun had been up an hour".
Agreement: the field is described as unrecognisable after eleven years of daily crossing, which makes the failure of the ordinary explicit.
Qualification: the writer supplies a natural explanation - the silence removing her sense of scale - so the rules have not stopped so much as lost their usual evidence.
Judgement: the effect works because the explanation arrives late; a reader who is given the cause first would find the passage merely descriptive.

blocks.heading: Section A checklist
items: Have I answered from the **lines the question names**?
Q1: four short answers, no sentences, nothing beyond four.
Q2: three quotations, each with a named effect, one developed further.
Q3: beginning, shift, end - and no language analysis smuggled in.
Q4: a stated position in sentence one, four paragraphs, one qualification.
Have I left 45 minutes for Section B?

blocks.heading: Questions students ask about Paper 1 Section A

items.q: How many quotations should I use in AQA Paper 1 Question 2?
a: Three short ones, each developed, is a reliable shape for 8 marks in about 10 minutes. The specimen mark scheme's top band asks for a judicious range of examples rather than a large number, so four undeveloped quotations score lower than three explained ones.

items.q: What counts as structure in Question 3?
a: Anything about the order and shape of the whole extract: what comes first, where the focus narrows or widens, shifts in time or place or perspective, repeated images, information withheld and released, and how the passage ends compared with how it began. Word choice and imagery belong in Question 2, not here.

items.q: Do I have to agree with the statement in Question 4?
a: No. You are asked to what extent you agree, and a well-argued partial disagreement scores as highly as agreement. What the marks reward is evaluation supported by references, not the position you take.

items.q: How long should my Question 4 answer be?
a: Long enough for four developed paragraphs, which in about 20 minutes is usually one to one and a half sides. Length is not marked, but 20 marks cannot realistically be earned in two short paragraphs.

hero.text: Four questions, forty marks. Two of them ask you to work across both sources at once, and that is where most of the difficulty and most of the marks sit.

blocks.title: Original RCF practice material
text: The two short sources below, and every question, practice task and model answer on this page, were written by RCF English. They are **not** AQA sources or AQA questions, and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced. AQA's own materials are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/).

blocks.text: **Section A of Paper 2 is 40 marks in four questions: 4, 8, 12 and 16.** Question 1 is retrieval. Question 2 is a summary across both sources. Question 3 is language analysis on one named source. Question 4 compares the two writers' attitudes and the methods they use to convey them.

blocks.heading: The two sources used in the examples below
text: Both are original passages written for this page, in the pattern Paper 2 uses: one 19th-century, one modern, on the same subject. **Neither is an AQA source.**

parts.heading: Source A (19th century, original RCF passage): from a letter on the walking of long distances, 1871
text: I am told by my nephew that the young men of this age no longer walk, and that where a journey of eight or ten miles is proposed they will contrive by some ingenuity to be carried. I do not doubt him. I observe it myself upon the roads.

It is said in their defence that time is short and business presses. I have heard this argument for forty years and I have never yet met the man whom it made happier. A journey on foot is not lost time. It is the only portion of the day in which a man is obliged to think consecutively, having nothing else whatever to do, and I hold that the quality of a man's thinking may be measured tolerably well by the number of miles he has walked alone.

There is besides the matter of the country itself. He who is carried through a district has seen it; he who has walked it knows it. He knows which of its hills is steeper than it looks, where the wind comes from, and which of its villages is glad to see a stranger. This is not knowledge of an ornamental kind. It is the only sort worth the name, being got by the body as well as the mind.

parts.heading: Source B (21st century, original RCF passage): from a magazine column on walking to work
text: For eleven weeks last year I walked to work. Fifty minutes each way, in weather that was frankly not always on my side, and I would like to report that it changed me. It did not change me. I am the same person, only with better calves and a slightly resentful relationship with rain.

What it did do was give me back a stretch of the day that nobody could book a meeting in. That turns out to be the whole of the benefit, and it is a considerable one. I did not have profound thoughts. Mostly I thought about lunch. But I thought about lunch *at my own speed*, which after four years of being interrupted every eleven minutes felt close to a holiday.

I am aware that this makes a poor advertisement. The people who write about walking tend to come back transfigured, striding down from some hill with their priorities rearranged. I came back with a damp coat. All I can honestly claim is that the fifty minutes were mine, and that when I stopped walking I noticed their absence more than I had noticed their presence.

parts.heading: What it is for and what it is worth
text: AO1. Eight statements are given about a numbered section of Source A, and you shade the boxes of the four that are true. 4 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 5 minutes.**

parts.heading: The method
numbered: Read only the lines the question names.
Test each statement against the text, not against what sounds reasonable.
Reject any statement that is *nearly* right - a single changed word makes it false.
Shade exactly four. Shading five can cost you a mark you had already earned.

parts.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Choosing a statement that is true of the world but not stated in those lines.
Choosing one that appears later in the source, outside the named lines.
Marking more than four boxes.
Spending ten minutes on four marks.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO1: select and synthesise evidence from different texts. You are asked for a summary of the differences or similarities between two things across both sources. It is a reading question, not a language question - do not analyse method here.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 8 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 8 minutes.** The specimen mark scheme's top band for this question is 7-8 marks and rewards perceptive synthesis and interpretation of both texts.

parts.heading: The method: state, evidence, infer, link
numbered: State the difference in your own words.
Give a short quotation from Source A.
Give a short quotation from Source B.
Infer - say what each quotation suggests. This is where the higher marks are.
Repeat for a second and third difference.

parts.heading: Worked example
text: *Write a summary of the differences between what the two writers gain from walking.*

The first writer believes walking improves the quality of a person's thinking, while the modern writer claims almost the opposite. The 1871 writer holds that "the quality of a man's thinking may be measured tolerably well by the number of miles he has walked alone", which suggests he sees walking as a discipline that produces better thought. The columnist reports that she "did not have profound thoughts" and "mostly thought about lunch", which suggests she found no such improvement and is unwilling to pretend she did.

They also differ in what they think walking teaches. The older writer values the knowledge of a place got "by the body as well as the mind", implying that walking gives a kind of understanding that being carried cannot. The columnist says nothing about knowing her route at all; what she gained was "a stretch of the day that nobody could book a meeting in", which suggests she values walking for the time it protects rather than for anything it reveals.

Finally, they differ in confidence. The first writer states his views as settled truths - "I hold that", "It is the only sort worth the name". The columnist undercuts hers - "this makes a poor advertisement", "All I can honestly claim" - which suggests a writer more interested in being accurate than persuasive.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: *Write a summary of the differences between the two writers' attitudes to other people's opinions of walking.* Use both sources. About 8 minutes.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO2, on one named source only. The question states the purpose the language serves - to influence, to persuade, to convey feeling - and asks how the writer's language does it. Answering on the wrong source scores nothing, so check which one is named.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 12 marks - half as much again as Paper 1 Question 2. **RCF recommendation: about 12 minutes.** The specimen mark scheme's top band is 10-12 marks and rewards detailed and perceptive understanding of language.

parts.heading: The method: the same as Paper 1 Q2, but four points and deeper
text: The extra four marks are not bought with extra quotations. They are bought by taking each quotation further - a second reading of a word, an observation about how one choice works against another, a comment on the cumulative effect across the extract.
numbered: Four short quotations rather than three.
For each: what the writer is doing, and the effect on the reader.
For at least two: a second layer - why *that* word rather than a near-synonym.
One closing sentence on the overall effect of the language across the whole extract.

parts.heading: Worked example (first two paragraphs)
text: *How does the writer of Source B use language to convey her attitude to walking?*

The writer's most consistent tool is deflation. She sets up an expectation and then punctures it: "I would like to report that it changed me. It did not change me." The second sentence is a flat repetition of the first with the verb reversed, and the plainness is the point - a writer wanting to convince us would have found a more graceful way to say it. The refusal of grace signals that she is more interested in being truthful than in being inspiring.

Her humour works the same way. She reports gaining "better calves and a slightly resentful relationship with rain", pairing a physical benefit with an emotional one that is deliberately trivial. "Resentful" is doing more than it appears to: it gives the rain a personality and gives her a grudge, which makes the whole eleven weeks sound like an argument she was having with the weather rather than a spiritual exercise. The effect is to keep the reader on her side while she declines to make the usual claims.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: *How does the writer of Source A use language to try to persuade the reader that walking is valuable?* Four developed paragraphs. About 12 minutes.

parts.heading: Indicative content for the practice task
bullets: **"contrive by some ingenuity to be carried"** - the elaborate phrasing mocks the effort young men put into avoiding effort.
**"I have heard this argument for forty years and I have never yet met the man whom it made happier"** - the long clause and the personal testimony present opinion as accumulated evidence.
**"He who is carried through a district has seen it; he who has walked it knows it"** - the balanced pair of clauses makes the distinction sound self-evident rather than argued.
**"not knowledge of an ornamental kind"** - dismissing the alternative as decorative implies his own view is practical, which is harder to disagree with.
Overall: the writer's certainty is created by structure - balanced sentences, flat assertions, no qualification anywhere.

parts.heading: What it is for
text: AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed, across two texts. Both halves are marked. An answer that compares only the attitudes, or only the methods, has answered half the question.

parts.heading: Marks and time
text: 16 marks. **RCF recommendation: about 20 minutes** - the largest share of the section. The specimen mark scheme's top band is 13-16 marks and rewards perceptive, detailed comparison of ideas and perspectives.

parts.heading: The method: one paragraph, both writers
text: The single most useful rule for this question: **never write a paragraph about only one source.** Each paragraph names a point of difference and handles both writers inside it.
numbered: Name the difference in attitude in your first sentence.
Writer A's attitude, with a short quotation, and the method that conveys it.
Writer B's attitude, with a short quotation, and the method that conveys it.
A sentence weighing them - who is more forceful, more honest, more likely to convince, and why.
Three paragraphs of this shape is a full answer.

parts.heading: Worked example (one full paragraph)
text: *Compare how the two writers convey their different attitudes to walking.*

The two writers differ most in how certain they allow themselves to sound. The 1871 writer conveys his attitude through unqualified assertion: "It is the only sort worth the name", he says of knowledge got on foot, and the absolute "only" leaves the reader no room to hold a different view politely. His balanced sentence structures - "he who is carried ... he who has walked" - present a personal preference in the shape of a proverb, which makes disagreement feel like disagreeing with common sense. The modern writer conveys her attitude by removing certainty wherever it appears. "All I can honestly claim" concedes the smallness of her case before the reader can object to it, and the admission that her account "makes a poor advertisement" turns a weakness into evidence of honesty. The older writer therefore persuades by sounding authoritative and the modern writer by sounding trustworthy - and because she has already agreed her claim is modest, she is the harder of the two to argue with.

parts.heading: Practice (original RCF task)
text: *Compare how the two writers convey their different attitudes to what walking is good for.* Three paragraphs, both writers in each. About 20 minutes.

blocks.heading: The comparison question
do: Handle both writers inside every paragraph.
Name the attitude before analysing the method.
Use comparative connectives: *whereas*, *by contrast*, *where A asserts, B concedes*.
Weigh the two at least once - which is more effective, and why.
Quote briefly and often rather than at length.
dont: Do not write three paragraphs on Source A and then three on Source B.
Do not list techniques without saying what attitude they convey.
Do not treat the older source as simply harder or worse written.
Do not summarise the sources - the summary was Question 2.
Do not run out of time; this is 16 marks and it comes last in the section.

blocks.heading: Questions students ask about Paper 2 Section A

items.q: What is the difference between Question 2 and Question 4 on AQA Paper 2?
a: Question 2 is a summary worth 8 marks and asks *what* the differences are, using inference from both sources. Question 4 is worth 16 marks and asks both what the writers' attitudes are and *how* they convey them - so it needs analysis of method as well as content. Writing a Question 2 style summary in answer to Question 4 caps the mark, because half the assessment objective is untouched.

items.q: How many paragraphs should a Question 4 answer have?
a: Three developed paragraphs, each covering both sources, is a reliable shape for 16 marks in about 20 minutes. More paragraphs usually means less development in each, which the mark scheme's top band does not reward.

items.q: Do I need to know anything about the 19th century?
a: No. Context is not assessed in English Language, and there are no marks for historical background. Read the older source for its argument and its tone in exactly the way you read the modern one.
Whichever one the question names - it is a single source, and it may be either. Check before you write, because analysing the other source thoroughly earns no marks at all.
